question: In which terms does an autothrottle control each engine's thrust?

options.text: N1, EPR or a target airspeed
N2, fuel quantity or Mach number
Fuel flow, EGT or oil pressure

explanation: The autothrottle positions the throttles to hold a value of fan speed (N1), engine pressure ratio (EPR) or a target airspeed set on the MCP.

question: Is there a direct indication of the thrust an engine is producing?

options.text: Only on engines with a FADEC
Yes; a thrust gauge in pounds or newtons
No; N1 or EPR is used as its measure
Yes; the fuel flow gauge shows it directly

explanation: Although thrust can be computed, there is as yet no direct thrust indicator; N1 and EPR are used as the measure of engine thrust.

question: Over which part of a flight can the autothrottle control thrust or speed?

options.text: From the take-off roll to after landing
From 400 ft after take-off to the outer marker only
From the take-off roll to 400 ft only
From top of climb to top of descent only

explanation: Using its modes the autothrottle can control thrust or speed from the beginning of the take-off roll until it is disconnected after an automatic landing.

question: What other name is used for the autothrottle system?
explanation: The autothrottle is also called the thrust management system, working with the autopilot and the FMS.

question: Which of these is an input to the autothrottle system?

options.text: Angle of attack from the AoA sensor
Cabin altitude from the pressure controller
Oil quantity from the engine sensors

explanation: Inputs include MCP mode selection, TAS, Mach and TAT from the ADC, attitude and acceleration from the IRS, N1 or EPR, angle of attack, radio altitude, air/ground logic, reverse demand, FMS thrust command, PLA and flap position.

question: Why does the autothrottle receive air/ground logic from the landing gear?

options.text: To retract the landing gear automatically after lift-off
To arm the reversers in flight
To know if it is on the ground or airborne

explanation: The landing gear switch tells the system whether the aircraft is on the ground or airborne, which changes which modes and functions are available.

question: Which of these is an output of the autothrottle system?

options.text: Signals to the throttle servo actuator
Signals to the fuel jettison valves in an emergency

explanation: Outputs go to the A/T servo actuator, the disengage circuit, BITE circuits, mode annunciation on EFIS, thrust limits to EICAS or ECAM, and failure warnings.

question: Why is there feedback from the autothrottle servo actuators to the computer?

options.text: To limit the fuel flow at take-off
To measure the engine thrust directly in pounds
To control how fast the levers move

explanation: The system compares actual and reference values and drives the lever servos; feedback from the servos controls the rate at which the thrust levers move.

question: In normal operation, what provides the autothrottle with its N1 limits?
explanation: In normal operation the FMC provides the autothrottle with the N1 limit values.

question: How are the thrust levers moved in a typical system?

options.text: By one servomotor driving both levers through a clutch
By a separate servomotor on each lever
By hydraulic jacks on the engines

explanation: Each thrust lever has its own servomotor, which allows the system to equalise N1 by moving each lever separately.

question: Does moving the thrust levers by hand normally disengage the autothrottle?

options.text: No, except a 10° split late on a dual approach
No, never under any circumstances at all

explanation: Manual positioning does not disengage it unless the levers are split by more than 10° during a dual channel approach after FLARE armed. Afterwards the A/T may reposition them, except in HOLD and ARM.

question: What does the main engine control (MEC) do?

options.text: It records engine data for the maintenance engineers
It schedules fuel for the thrust lever setting

explanation: The hydromechanical MEC schedules fuel to give the thrust called for by the thrust lever setting.

question: What does the power management control (PMC) do?

options.text: Trims the MEC electronically to obtain the desired N1
Moves the thrust levers to the N1 limit by servomotor

explanation: The PMC refines the fuel flow electronically, without moving the thrust levers, using power lever angle, N1, inlet temperature and pressure.

question: What does the PMC's constant thrust climb feature give?

options.text: A constant rate of climb with varying thrust
Climb thrust held without moving the levers
A constant airspeed through pitch changes
A constant fuel flow in the climb

explanation: Once the lever is set for climb, the PMC keeps that thrust throughout the climb with no further lever adjustment.

question: How does the PMC signal a detectable failure?

options.text: A red warning and a fire bell
An instant N1 drop to idle
No warning is given; the MEC takes over silently
A slow N1 drift, then PMC INOP and cautions

explanation: The PMC schedules a slow N1 drift over about 30 seconds, then lights PMC INOP, the ENG annunciator and the MASTER CAUTION lights.

question: After a PMC is switched off, what controls engine speed?
explanation: With the PMC selected off, engine speed is controlled by the hydromechanical MEC alone.

question: For autothrottle use, how should the two PMCs be set?

options.text: Both OFF for take-off, ON for landing
It makes no difference at all

explanation: The A/T works with PMCs on or off, but both on or both off gives the least thrust lever separation. A/T take-offs may be made with both off.

question: How is the autothrottle armed?

options.text: By pressing TO/GA on the ground before take-off
By selecting a speed on the MCP
By moving the A/T Arm switch to ARM

explanation: The A/T Arm switch at ARM arms it for engagement in N1, MCP SPD or FMC SPD. The switch is held magnetically and releases to OFF on disengagement.

question: Which of these disengages the autothrottle?

options.text: Engaging the second autopilot on the approach

explanation: The A/T disengages on the arm switch to OFF, either disengage switch, a system fault, 2 s after touchdown, or more than 10° lever split on a dual approach after FLARE.

question: What indicates that the autothrottle has disengaged?

options.text: The thrust levers move to idle
The arm switch releases to OFF and the A/T light flashes red
The arm switch stays at ARM and a green light shows on the MCP

explanation: Disengagement is followed by the A/T Arm switch releasing to OFF and the A/T Disengage light flashing red.

question: After an automatic disengagement after landing, does the A/T disengage light come on?
explanation: The A/T Disengage lights do not illuminate when the A/T disengages automatically after landing.

question: Which conditions engage the autothrottle take-off mode?

options.text: At 84 kt, with the levers set by hand
On the ground, A/T armed, TO/GA pressed
In flight below 2000 ft, TO/GA pressed
On the ground, with the autopilot engaged in CMD

explanation: Pressing either TOGA switch on the ground with the A/T armed and the take-off N1 limit selected on the CDU engages take-off mode; the annunciation changes from ARM to N1.

question: During the take-off roll, what does THR HLD mean?

options.text: The levers are locked against any movement
The A/T is holding the speed target
The pilot, not the A/T, may move the levers
The thrust has been reduced to climb

explanation: THR HLD annunciates at about 84 kt (64 kt on earlier computers): the autothrottle will not change the lever position, but the levers can be moved by hand.

question: In a typical system, at what speed does THR HLD annunciate in the take-off roll?
explanation: THR HLD appears at about 84 kt, or 64 kt with earlier autothrottle computers.

question: After lift-off, when does the autothrottle change from THR HLD to ARM?

options.text: When the landing gear is retracted after take-off
Above 400 ft RA and about 18 s after lift-off

explanation: The A/T stays in THR HLD until 400 ft RA and about 18 seconds after lift-off, then changes to ARM. Climb thrust can then be selected with the N1 switch.

question: For how long after lift-off is automatic reduction to climb thrust inhibited in LVL CHG or V/S?
explanation: Automatic reduction is inhibited for 2½ minutes in LVL CHG or V/S. If VNAV, ALT ACQ or ALT HOLD engages in this period, the reduction occurs normally.

question: In N1 mode, what does the autothrottle hold?

options.text: A fixed EPR set by the crew on the panel
The N1 limit selected on the FMC CDU

explanation: In N1 mode the A/T holds thrust at the N1 limit selected on the CDU. Pressing the N1 switch again changes the mode to ARM.

question: An engine fails with the autothrottle in N1 mode. What does its thrust lever do?

options.text: Advances a little, then returns to the other
Advances to the full forward stop and stays there

explanation: The failed engine's lever advances a few degrees then returns to or below the other lever's position.

question: In MCP SPD mode, which speed is the target?

options.text: The speed at the moment of engagement only
The speed or Mach in the MCP display

explanation: The speed or Mach shown in the MCP IAS/Mach display is the target. The A/T will not exceed the displayed N1 limit.

question: An engine fails with the autothrottle in a speed mode. What happens?

options.text: The failed engine's lever goes back to idle
Both levers advance to hold the speed

explanation: Both thrust levers advance together to maintain the target speed.

question: What autothrottle approach speed is recommended in landing configuration?
explanation: The A/T corrects for normal gusts through speed and acceleration sensing, so wind additives are not recommended; VREF + 5 is the setting. Higher settings give excessive approach speed.

question: In FMC SPD mode, where is the target speed shown?

options.text: By the speed cursors; MCP display blank
On the FMS control unit's performance page only

explanation: In FMC SPD, commanded by the FMC in VNAV, the MCP display is blank and the cursors show the FMC speed. Thrust is limited to the N1 on the thrust mode annunciator.

question: Up to what thrust lever separation will the autothrottle try to equalise N1?
explanation: The A/T equalises N1 through individual lever control, limited to 8° of lever separation.

question: When is ARM annunciated for the autothrottle?

options.text: The switch is at ARM and no A/T mode is engaged
The autothrottle is retarding the levers to idle

explanation: ARM shows with the switch at ARM and no mode engaged; the levers can then be moved by hand without interference.

question: In which descents does the autothrottle annunciate RETARD?
explanation: RETARD engages in LVL CHG and VNAV descents and changes to ARM when the levers reach the aft stop or are held from reaching it.

question: When does the landing flare RETARD engage?

options.text: At 50 ft RA, on every landing
2½ s after FLARE, or 27 ft RA if sooner

explanation: During landing, RETARD engages 2½ seconds after FLARE engagement or at 27 ft RA, whichever comes first.

question: On a visual approach with landing flap and no ALT ACQ or ALT HOLD, when does RETARD engage?
explanation: For a non-precision or visual approach with flaps 15 or more and the AFDS not in ALT ACQ or ALT HOLD, RETARD engages at 27 ft RA.

question: When is the autothrottle go-around mode armed?

options.text: Below 1500 ft, with the autopilot engaged in CMD
At any height with TO/GA pressed
Below 2000 ft RA, with the switch at ARM

explanation: The A/T GA mode arms below 2000 ft RA with the switch at ARM, with or without the AFDS engaged, and can be used until 2 s after touchdown.

question: Pressing TO/GA once in an autothrottle go-around gives what thrust?

options.text: Full go-around thrust at once, for maximum climb

explanation: The levers advance to reduced GA thrust, giving 1000–2000 fpm climb. A second press advances to the full GA N1 limit.

question: How is full go-around thrust selected?

options.text: By pressing TO/GA a second time
By moving the levers to the stop

explanation: After reaching reduced GA thrust, a second press of TO/GA signals the A/T to advance to the full go-around N1 limit.

question: In a single-engine flight director go-around, what thrust does the autothrottle set?
explanation: With one engine the A/T increases thrust to the full N1 limit.

question: How can the autothrottle go-around mode be ended?

options.text: By a new pitch mode, or at ALT ACQ
Automatically at 1000 ft above the field elevation
By pressing TO/GA a third time

explanation: After reaching reduced or full GA thrust, selecting another AFDS pitch mode or ALT ACQ engaging ends the A/T GA mode.

question: What does a flashing amber A/T disengage light indicate?

options.text: The thrust levers are split by more than 10°
The red filament test is selected

explanation: In flight, flaps not up and in MCP SPD or FMC SPD, a flashing amber light shows the A/T is not holding speed within +10 or −5 kt of the command.

question: How do you extinguish the autothrottle warning after an automatic disengagement?

options.text: Move the thrust levers to idle

explanation: After automatic disengagement, pressing the A/T disengage switch (or the light, or re-arming) extinguishes the warning.

question: How does the automatic test of the flashing amber function appear?

options.text: Flashing 2 s, off 2 s, flashing 2 s
Steady amber for 10 seconds, then off

explanation: With the A/T in a speed mode, more than 150 s after lift-off with flaps extended, the amber light flashes 2 s, goes out 2 s, then flashes 2 s.

question: Where is the thrust mode annunciator panel located in a typical system?

options.text: On the glareshield, beside the mode control panel
Centre panel, above the N1 indicators

explanation: It sits on the centre instrument panel above the N1 indicators and shows the active N1 limit reference mode.

question: When is A/T LIM annunciated?

options.text: When FMC N1 limits are invalid
When the autothrottle is limiting the speed to VMO
When the levers reach the forward stop

explanation: A/T LIM appears when FMC N1 limits are invalid or either engine N1 is below 18%; the A/T computer then calculates a single N1 limit.

question: What is the purpose of a flexible (reduced thrust) take-off?

options.text: To save time on a long runway
To reduce engine wear and extend engine life
To shorten the take-off distance on a long runway

explanation: When full power is not needed, as at light weight on a long runway, reduced power lowers engine wear and increases engine life.

question: How is reduced take-off thrust set with an autothrottle?

options.text: By selecting climb thrust on the runway
By reducing the take-off weight entered
By entering a higher assumed temperature
By entering a pressure altitude higher than the airfield's

explanation: Selecting an assumed temperature higher than ambient makes the thrust computation produce a lower EPR or N1 limit.

question: May the autothrottle be used in light to moderate turbulence?

options.text: No, it must be disengaged in any turbulence

explanation: The A/T may stay engaged in light to moderate turbulence unless performance is poor. Expect more lever activity and speed excursions of 10–15 kt.

question: Which speed excursions are expected with the autothrottle in moderate turbulence?
explanation: Increased thrust lever activity and airspeed excursions of 10 to 15 kt are to be expected. The A/T is not used in severe turbulence.

question: What does FADEC stand for?

options.text: Full automatic display of engine conditions

explanation: FADEC provides complete engine management throughout all phases of flight.

question: Which of these is a FADEC function?

options.text: Over-speed protection of N1 and N2

explanation: FADEC controls gas generation, protects engine limits (N1 and N2 over-speed), manages power, and runs automatic and manual start sequences.

question: During a manual engine start, what does the FADEC do?

options.text: It controls the whole start sequence automatically

explanation: In a manual start the FADEC passively monitors the start valve, fuel, ignition, N1, N2, fuel flow and EGT. In an automatic start it controls them.

question: Which is an advantage of FADEC?

options.text: It removes the need for thrust levers
It allows engines to run without fuel pumps
It saves fuel and improves engine life

explanation: FADEC reduces workload, protects engine limits, improves engine life and saves fuel and maintenance time.

question: How many FADEC channels does each engine have?

options.text: Three, voting two out of three for each engine
Two, one in control and one in standby

explanation: There are two FADEC channels per engine, one controlling and one on standby for redundancy.

question: What powers the FADEC once the engine is above about 12% rpm?

options.text: The aircraft AC supply through the main bus

explanation: Each channel uses aircraft AC before and during the initial start, then its own magnetic alternator above about 12% engine rpm.

question: What does the fuel metering valve do in a FADEC system?

options.text: Shuts off fuel in a fire
Turns FADEC orders into fuel flow
Measures the fan speed, N1, for the FADEC

explanation: The FMV converts FADEC orders, through a torque motor and servo valve, into fuel flow. Its resolver sends position feedback, and a bypass valve keeps the pressure drop constant.

question: To hold a target N1, what does the FADEC allow to vary?

options.text: N2, within its minimum and maximum
EGT, without any limit being applied

explanation: The FADEC computes the fuel flow to hold target N1, letting N2 vary between N2 min and N2 max, and adjusts N2/N1 for load, bleed demand and to avoid stalls or flameout.

question: In a FADEC system with fixed detents, how are the thrust levers moved?
explanation: Unlike many autothrottle systems, the levers are only moved by hand. Their position goes to the FADEC, which computes the rating limit and N1.

question: How many detents divide the thrust lever sector in such a system?
explanation: The sector is divided into four segments by five detents or stops. There is no reverse idle detent.

question: With the thrust lever between two detents, which rating limit does the FADEC select?
explanation: In a detent, the FADEC selects that detent's limit; between two detents it selects the limit of the higher mode.

question: On the ground with the lever in FLX-MCT, when is flex take-off thrust selected?

options.text: Always, regardless of any entry in the MCDU
When a flex temperature above TAT is set

explanation: Flex rating is selected if a flex temperature greater than the current TAT has been entered in the MCDU; otherwise MCT is selected.

question: After take-off, how is the rating changed from FLX to MCT?

options.text: Pressing the autothrust button on the glareshield
Lever to TO/GA or CL, then back to MCT

explanation: Moving the lever to TO/GA or CL and back to MCT changes FLX to MCT; flex cannot then be reselected.

question: In such a system, how is maximum take-off thrust always available?

options.text: By pushing the lever fully forward
By selecting a lower flex temperature

explanation: MAX TO thrust is always available by pushing the thrust lever fully forward.

question: In automatic (autothrust) mode, how is the thrust limited?

options.text: To idle, until the pilot moves the thrust lever
To the FMGC value, with no limit
To the lever position's value, except alpha floor

explanation: The FMGC computes the thrust, limited to the value corresponding to the lever position, unless alpha floor protection is active.
